summary: Ukraine strikes deep into Russia as Trump pauses sanctions, Egypt edges toward Yemen's war, France counts riot damage, China's exports lift growth, and AI debt wobbles.

topics.heading: Ukraine hits St Petersburg in a huge drone attack as Trump pauses new Russia sanctions
topics.summary: Russia says it stopped 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight; strikes hit an oil terminal and depot in St Petersburg, killing one person. Trump defended pausing new sanctions on Moscow and said Zelenskyy "doesn't want to end this war".

lead.title: Ukraine launches over 1,000 drones at Russia, setting oil facilities ablaze

alsoReported.title: Russia's war on Ukraine 'must be brought to an end', Zelenskyy says

article: Overnight into Sunday, Ukraine launched what Russia's defence ministry called 1,015 drones at 15 Russian regions, Crimea and the Black Sea, all of which it says were "neutralised"[^1]. Even so, St Petersburg's governor said drones hit the city's oil terminal, an oil depot and warehouses, killing at least one person and injuring five; the airport restricted flights, and about 20,000 people in the surrounding region lost power[^1]. Russian state media called it the largest attack on the city since 2022[^2].

The strike came as Ukraine and the US openly disagree. On Friday, President Donald Trump waived parts of a new law that targets Russia's energy income; Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump wants up to 60 days to study the economic effects[^2]. Trump said he did not want to drive Moscow "away from the bargaining table", criticised Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil, and wrote that Zelenskyy "doesn't want to end this war"[^1][^2].

Ukraine's case is that it is answering Russia's own energy campaign. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia hit Ukraine's energy, oil and gas sites 76 times in the week after Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" on October 11, and used almost 2,700 attack drones in a week[^1]. He also said US intelligence sharing has resumed after a pause, and that talks with US envoys continue[^1][^2].

Why it matters: both sides are now trying to damage the other's energy system before winter, and the main outside player is pressing the side that was invaded. My read: Kyiv is betting that hurting Russia's oil income gives it more leverage than waiting on Washington, and that is a risk if US support keeps cooling.
topics.differences: Russia says it stopped all 1,015 drones; St Petersburg officials still report a death, fires and power cuts[^1]. Trump frames Ukraine's strikes as an obstacle to peace; Zelenskyy frames them as a reply to Russia's strikes during a truce he says Russia ignored[^1][^2].

topics.heading: Egypt moves toward sending troops to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
topics.summary: Egypt's president asked parliament to approve sending forces abroad after pledging "all possible" support to Saudi Arabia, which faces near-daily Houthi missile and drone attacks. The Houthis warned Cairo to stay out.

lead.title: Egypt pledges support for Saudi Arabia as Houthis warn Cairo against military intervention

alsoReported.title: Egypt's president vows to use 'any measure' to defend Saudi Arabia and seeks authorization to deploy troops abroad as battle against Houthis escalates

article: Egypt's National Defence Council, chaired by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, pledged "all necessary and possible forms of support" to Saudi Arabia, and Sisi asked parliament on Saturday to authorise sending troops and equipment abroad[^3][^4]. Egypt's constitution requires a two-thirds vote for that; parliament met Sunday and resumes Monday[^3][^4]. Sisi said Egypt would act only if Riyadh asks, and approval alone would not mean troops are sent[^3].

Background: the Houthis, an Iran-backed movement that controls much of northern Yemen, have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's recognised government. AP says the fighting has reignited Yemen's civil war after four years of ceasefire[^4]. A Saudi-led coalition spokesman says Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have killed 19 people since October 1[^3]. On Sunday the Houthi-run health ministry said an airstrike in Saada killed at least nine people, including five children, and blamed Saudi Arabia, which had not commented[^4].

It sits inside the wider Iran war. On Monday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said another oil tanker caught fire after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, and Russia's foreign minister Sergei Lavrov was due in Tehran[^5]. Iran says it is reviewing a US reply to its proposal to end the eight-month war[^4].

Why it matters: Egypt has the Arab world's largest army and lost heavily in Yemen in the 1960s, which commentators cite as a reason for caution[^3]. My read: if Cairo does send forces, a Gulf conflict that began between Iran, Israel and the US would draw in another major state, making a negotiated end harder.
topics.differences: Riyadh's coalition describes the Houthi strikes as attacks on civilians and airports, and the UN Security Council called them "escalatory"[^3]. The Houthis say Saudi Arabia has waged "aggression and siege" on Yemen for over 12 years and warned Egypt that joining would endanger its own security[^3].

topics.heading: France counts the damage after its worst rioting in years; Macron promises accountability
topics.summary: Protests over living costs and schools turned violent on Saturday, with looting and a city hall burned in Limoges. Arrest counts range from 1,800 to about 2,400. Macron spoke of "anger and shame" but declared no emergency.

lead.title: 'Anger and shame': Macron denounces France's nationwide rioting, looting

alsoReported.title: French police arrest more than 1,800 people after violent protests erupt across country

article: Saturday's nationwide marches over living costs and underfunded schools were followed by looting and fires in several cities. In Limoges, the 19th-century City Hall burned and its roof collapsed; the local prefect said the fire was set on purpose[^6]. The interior minister said hundreds of businesses were looted in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux[^6].

Numbers depend on who counts and when. AP reported at least 1,800 arrests and more than 500 police, gendarmes and firefighters injured on Saturday; by Sunday, Al Jazeera cited the Interior Ministry at nearly 2,400 arrests and about 1,000 officers injured[^6][^7]. Authorities put the crowds at about 550,000, organisers at about 800,000[^6].

In a televised address on Sunday, President Emmanuel Macron spoke of "anger and shame", separated protesters with "legitimate demands" from those who looted, and promised a crisis unit for people in difficulty; he did not declare a state of emergency or a curfew[^7]. He has blamed "insurrectionist elements" from the radical far left, joined by criminals[^6].

Why it matters: France votes for a new president next spring, and every camp is using the unrest[^6][^7]. My read: the deeper issue, how to fund schools and services while cutting a deficit, was there before the riots and will still be there after them.
topics.differences: Macron blames radical far-left groups and criminals[^6]. Left-wing leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon says the government is "solely responsible"; far-right figure Jordan Bardella called Macron's speech "cowardly"[^7]. US President Trump linked the unrest to immigration; AP notes French authorities have made no such link[^6].

topics.heading: China's economy grows 4.5% in the third quarter, carried by exports
topics.summary: Growth beat forecasts and rose from 4.3% the quarter before, but most of the lift came from exports. Retail sales grew just 1.1% and property investment is down 20.6% this year.

lead.title: China's economy accelerated in the July-September quarter on robust exports

alsoReported.title: China Q3 GDP beats forecasts at 4.5%, retail sales grow at fastest pace since March

article: China said on Monday that its economy grew 4.5% in July to September compared with a year earlier, slightly better than economists expected and up from 4.3% in the spring, the slowest pace in more than three years[^8][^9]. Growth for the first nine months was 4.6%, inside Beijing's 2026 target of 4.5% to 5%[^9].

Exports did most of the work. AP reports exports rose 36% in September and the trade surplus reached $938 billion from January to September, on track to pass last year's record[^8]. At home the picture is weaker: retail sales, a measure of shopping, grew 1.1% in September; investment in property fell 20.6% so far this year[^9]. A statistics bureau official said weak domestic demand remains a "prominent problem"[^8].

Why it matters: when the world's second-largest economy grows by selling far more than it buys, other countries feel it. The EU runs a trade deficit with China of more than $1.1 billion a day, AP says, and has moved to limit some Chinese car imports[^8]. One Cornell economist told AP this reliance on foreign demand is unsustainable; others expect exports to stay strong[^8]. My read: the headline number is fine, but how households in China feel about money matters more for what comes next.

topics.heading: Investors sour on the debt paying for AI data centres in a rough week for tech
topics.summary: Shares of AI cloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius fell more than 25% last week and some data-centre bonds slid well below face value. Bulls call it "just another scare"; skeptics question whether AI revenue can cover the debt.

lead.title: 'Just another scare': Wall Street sees the AI trade strong despite tech's latest rout

alsoReported.title: Investors turn on the debt behind the AI build-out

article: Tech stocks ended last week lower as worries grew about how the AI building boom is being paid for. CoreWeave and Nebius, which rent out AI computing power, each closed the week down more than 25%, and Oracle was also hit[^10]. Analysts pointed to higher borrowing costs and "circular" deals, in which AI firms invest in customers that then buy their products[^10].

The pressure is clearest in debt. Citing the Financial Times, Enterprise reports that bonds tied to big data-centre projects have fallen below what they were issued at, that one CoreWeave bond fell under 80 cents on the dollar, and that a research firm counts at least 47 large US projects delayed, withdrawn or blocked this year[^11]. An Allianz executive called it a "Darwin moment" for weaker borrowers[^11].

Not everyone is worried. Wedbush's Dan Ives called it the "same script, different cast", UBS called it a "recalibration of expectations", and chipmakers ASML and TSMC still report strong demand[^10]. The same report says OpenAI's revenue came in below guidance and Anthropic's third-quarter growth fell short of expectations, though its revenue still rose about 50%[^11]. Disclosure: Anthropic makes the AI that writes this brief.

Why it matters: trillions of dollars of planned spending on chips, power and buildings depend on AI earning enough to repay the loans. My read: one bad week proves little, but the question has moved from whether AI works to whether it pays.
topics.differences: Bulls such as Wedbush and UBS see a temporary scare after big gains[^10]. Skeptics cited in the FT's reporting warn that AI revenue may not cover the debt and that much of the planned build may never happen[^11].

question.text: Investors are pulling back from the loans that pay for AI data centres. If building slows, who besides the AI companies would feel it first, and how might that reach someone in Toronto?
